transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-07
Start: 16:00 PDT
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Alex Park (Redwood AE), Samira Patel (Redwood SE), Mark Reynolds (Cedar Tech, CTO), Priya Singh (Cedar Tech, Senior ML Eng), Luis Gomez (Cedar Tech, Platform Eng)

Summary:
Quick hosted API walkthrough focused on chat/text generation basics: streaming responses, common parameters (temperature, top_p, max_tokens), retry/backoff behavior and idempotency, brief Console tour for observability and Optimize suggestions. Customer interested in latency targets for chat (p95 < 300ms on short responses), data residency and KMS, and a pilot to validate cost and throughput.

Topics:
- Hosted API endpoints for chat and text generation
- Streaming vs non-streaming behavior and SDK usage
- Request params (temperature, top_p, n, stop, max_tokens) and typical defaults
- Retries, idempotency keys, and recommended backoff for 429s/error handling
- Console demo: per-route metrics, token-level cost breakdown
- Redwood Optimize suggestions: batching, caching, quantization recommendations (overview)
- Security: SOC2, KMS, log masking, VPC/Dedicated options discussed at high level

Action items (captured during call): see metadata field.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Alex (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we, uh, we really appreciate you making time. Quick intro - I'm Alex, AE on the hosted API team, with Samira who's our solutions engineer. How are you doing Mark?
[00:08] Mark (Cedar Tech): Good thanks, Alex. Excited to see the demo. Briefly, Priya and Luis are on to cover ML and infra questions.
[00:14] Samira (Redwood SE): Awesome, quick agenda — we'll run through the hosted chat/text endpoints, show streaming, talk parameters, then Console for observability and a bit on Optimize. We'll leave time for questions.
[00:26] Priya (Cedar Tech): Sounds good — we're especially curious about p95 latency on short chat responses, and how retries are handled.
[00:33] Alex: Great, we'll try to hit that.

[01:05] Samira: Alright, starting with the API — the chat endpoint is basically a single REST call where you provide a messages array, model name, and params like temperature. For JavaScript/Python we have SDK helpers. The streaming option sends chunked events over an HTTP stream, so you can render tokens as they arrive.
[01:25] Mark: Is streaming SSE or websockets?
[01:29] Samira: It's SSE-style chunked HTTP by default, there's also streaming via websockets in our SDK if you prefer low-level control. In practice SSE covers most web clients.

[02:10] Priya: How do you recommend handling partial generations with streaming? e.g., final token vs intermediary tokens and hallucination checks?
[02:18] Samira: Good question. We recommend treating the stream as optimistic updates — show typing indicator, then final chunk includes complete finish_reason. For hallucinations we surface model confidence heuristics in Optimize but primary guardrails are prompt engineering and evals.

[03:00] Alex: Quick demo — I'll send a sample request using our JS SDK. (shares link to gist)
[03:10] Alex: Example: client.chat.create({ model: "redwood-large-v1", messages: [...], temperature: 0.2, top_p: 0.9, max_tokens: 150, stream: true }) — that's a typical low-temp chat setup for deterministic answers.
[03:30] Luis: That model name, is it hosted only? Can we pin versions?
[03:36] Samira: Yes hosted models are in the catalog, and you can pin a specific version/variant for consistent behavior. We also expose quantized variants for cost/latency tradeoffs.

[04:15] Mark: About latency — we want p95 under 300ms for short replies (<40 tokens). Any numbers you can share?
[04:23] Samira: For small responses we've seen p95 in the 150–350ms band on our hosted infra for `redwood-small/medium` variants; larger models and longer seqs increase this. We also have burst capacity options and regional routing to lower latency. I did add a note — these are workload dependent; best to run a short POC.

[05:10] Priya: Ok, what happens when we hit 429s or transient errors? What's the recommended retry strategy?
[05:18] Samira: Use exponential backoff with jitter, initial retry after ~200–500ms, double each time, and include an idempotency key for requests that are non-idempotent or if you need dedupe. For streaming requests, reconnect logic in the SDK handles resume semantics — but we recommend stateless request design when possible. Also we return Retry-After headers on rate limits.

[06:00] Alex: And we have client-side examples in the SDK for this pattern. We'll send those snippets in email.

[07:12] Luis: On auth and security — we currently use company KMS and need to know if Redwood can integrate with our KMS for key wrapping, and whether logs are encrypted at rest.
[07:22] Samira: Yes, for Private/Dedicated we support customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM). For hosted we use envelope encryption and support managed KMS integrations for select customers — we'll share the security whitepaper. Logs are encrypted at rest and we provide options for masked or redacted request logs.

[08:05] Mark: SOC2 and audit logs?
[08:09] Alex: Redwood is SOC2 Type II compliant; we provide audit logs, and for enterprise we can enable longer retention and SSO/SAML and RBAC. We'll attach the SOC2 attestation.

[09:00] Samira: Moving on — Console demo. (shares console link) Here you can see per-route latency, token-level cost, usage graphs, and per-model breakdown. If you turn on streaming you'll see request durations drop in the front-end because you render tokens earlier.
[09:28] Priya: Is there a way to see token-level profiling per request?
[09:32] Samira: Yes there's a request inspector, though for privacy we mask user PII in logs by default. You can opt-in to more detailed logs under enterprise contracts.

[10:15] Alex: Quick note on billing — hosted usage is per-token; we also charge small per-request overhead in some plans. For predicted cost reduction we have Redwood Optimize suggestions, which I'll show briefly.

[11:00] Samira: Optimize looks at your workload patterns and suggests batching, prefix caching, and model/quantization changes. For chat, prefix/KV caching can significantly reduce tokens on repeated system prompts or instruction-heavy contexts.
[11:20] Luis: How does caching play with privacy? We have sensitive PII — can cache be disabled or encrypted?
[11:26] Samira: Yes caches can be disabled per-route. For sensitive data we recommend disabling inference caching; for dedicated/private you can enable encrypted caches with customer keys.

[12:05] Mark: Could you walk through retry idempotency in the Console or logging?
[12:12] Samira: In logs we show request ids and idempotency_key if provided. The inspector will show retries and status codes; you can filter for 429s.

[13:00] (demo interruption, slight crosstalk)
[13:12] Alex: Sorry — small lag on my side, sharing a sample stream now.
[13:20] Samira: (typing) Example stream — you can see chunks arriving, each chunk has a token and optional finish_reason. For UI we recommend assembling tokens until finish_reason is done.

[15:00] Priya: For our chat orchestration we sometimes need to do partial re-rolls (n parameter >1). Does streaming support multiple candidates?
[15:07] Samira: Yes, streaming supports n>1 but it changes UX; the stream interleaves candidates, so usually we stream best-of-1 and request additional non-streamed completions for re-rolls. There's also logprobs support if you want to pick highest-scoring token sequences client-side.

[17:10] Mark: Any SDK differences between JS and Python for streaming?
[17:15] Samira: The semantics are similar; Python uses iterator-style yields, JS uses event callbacks or async iterators. We have code samples for both.

[19:00] Luis: What's the best practice for handling long-running streams and connection resets?
[19:06] Samira: Reconnect and resume is limited — we recommend short-lived streams and checkpointing. If you need guaranteed exactly-once generation, use synchronous (non-stream) calls with idempotency keys and wait for server confirmation.

[21:00] Alex: Let's touch on model selection — for lower latency and cost use smaller quantized variants; for highest quality use the larger models but expect higher token cost. Optimize can point you to a candidate model mix.

[22:10] Priya: Do you expose kernel or runtime details anywhere? We run perf-sensitive workloads and may want per-GPU metrics.

[22:20] Samira: We don't expose kernel internals, but we provide latency and throughput metrics per model variant and region. For Dedicated we give more telemetry.

[24:00] Mark: On data residency — our legal team requires EU data to remain in EU. Do you support region pinning?
[24:08] Samira: Yes region routing and model variants in EU region; for strict residency we recommend Dedicated or Private. Hosted supports region selection for enterprise agreements.

[26:30] Priya: If we run a POC, what's minimal scope? We want to test 50k qpm of chat with typical 60-token responses to validate cost and p95.
[26:40] Alex: For POC we'll need a traffic profile CSV, sample prompts, and success criteria (latency p95, cost per 1k tokens). We'll provision burst capacity and run benchmarks. Target start date discussed in action items.

[28:00] (short pause, background noise on one line)
[29:10] Luis: A quick security qu — do you support SSO for console access?
[29:14] Samira: Yes SAML/SSO and RBAC; we can map groups and roles.

[31:00] Priya: Any notes on safeguards for hallucinations and safety filters?
[31:06] Samira: We offer content filters and can integrate post-processing safety checks. For critical workflows we'd run evals and set up Canary rollouts via the Console.

[33:45] Mark: Competitors — we are also talking to OpenAI and Anthropic, any differentiators?
[33:52] Alex: People come to Redwood for predictable serving economics and unified runtime across hosted/dedicated/private; our focus is production tooling (Optimize, Console, rollouts) and predictable latency SLOs. We'll send a short competitive one-pager.

[35:00] Priya: Ok, pricing — can you give us a ballpark for hosted at our scale?
[35:06] Alex: Ballpark depends on model mix; for mid-sized model we estimate X tokens cost/1k and with caching/batching Optimize can cut effective cost 20–50% depending on workload. We'll provide a detailed pricing worksheet.

[36:40] Samira: One last note on retries for streaming clients — the SDK automatically does limited reconnect attempts, but if you see persistent 429s it's usually a sign to increase client side backoff or request dedicated capacity.

[38:00] Mark: Great, thanks. Any outstanding items from your side?
[38:06] Alex: We'll send pricing, SOC2, KMS notes, SDK retry examples, and propose POC timeline.

[40:00] (wrap up)
[40:05] Alex: Recap — 1) Alex to send pricing + burst/dedicated notes, 2) Samira to send security docs and SDK snippets, 3) Cedar to send traffic profile. Plan POC start week of 2026-08-17.
[40:30] Mark: Sounds good, thanks both.
[40:36] Luis: Thanks.
[40:40] Samira: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with calendar invites for the POC kickoff.
[40:46] (call ends)

Notes on transcription quality: some model names may be slightly transcribed (e.g., redwood-large-v1 vs redwood-large-v1-quant), minor speaker attribution errors possible.
